items.title: Fed's Goolsbee Warns Stubborn Inflation Could Force More Aggressive Rate Hikes — 'We're Not On Path Back To 2%'
items.excerpt: "If you look at how broad based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way," he said, while noting that there were some signs of trouble now for several months in a row. Goolsbee flagged services inflation and elevated healthcare costs, arguing that they are unlikely to ease simply because energy prices decline. "For me, keeping an eye on services inflation, which probably is not coming from tariffs or oil, is are some of the more troubling aspects of the inflation reports we've been getting for the last several months," he said. Goolsbee also cautioned against interpreting wage growth as an early warning sign of inflation, saying it tends to follow price increases rather than precede them. "Wage growth is not a leading indicator of inflation. It's actually a lagging indicator of inflation," he said.

items.title: Inflation will be key to future interest rate decisions: US Fed official
items.excerpt: Nov 15, 2026 San Diego [US], November 15: US Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip N Jefferson has said that inflation will be the key factor in determining future interest rate decisions, as price pressures remain elevated despite signs of stability in the American economy and labour market. Speaking at the University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable on Friday, Jefferson said, "Accordingly, I see the trajectory of inflation as providing the more important signal for determining the appropriate stance of monetary policy." He added, "Going forward, I believe that further policy adjustments should be determined by carefully examining trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks." Jefferson's remarks come as US inflation continues to remain well above the Federal Reserve's 2 per cent target. According to the data cited in his speech, the annual personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation rate stood at 3.6 per cent in September, while core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, was 3.1 per cent. Expressing concern over persistent price pressures, Jefferson said, "I remain concerned about the risk of higher energy prices leading to a persistent rise in inflation more broadly." He noted that higher energy costs were affecting sectors such as airfares and transportation, while strong demand for new technologies was also pushing up prices of certain goods, including memory chips. Jefferson said inflation data received so far for October remained consistent with price pressures staying well above the Fed's target. On the labour market, he said conditions had stabilised, with the unemployment rate standing at 4.1 per cent in October. "I expect the unemployment rate to stay around its current level in the near term-a level I view as consistent with maximum employment," he said. Jefferson also noted that the US economy had gained momentum this year, with gross domestic product (GDP) expanding at an annualised rate of 3.4 per cent in the third quarter. "The economy has gained momentum this year, expanding at a pace roughly in line with its potential," he said. Referring to the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) October meeting, Jefferson said he had joined the majority of policymakers in voting to keep interest rates unchanged. He said economic activity and labour market conditions had remained broadly solid since that meeting, while inflation readings continued to show persistent price pressures.

items.title: Trump’s judge appointment blitz faces Republican resistance By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 15 (Reuters) - A last-minute effort by US President Donald Trump to install as many judges as possible before Democrats take control of the US Senate is running into resistance from some fellow Republicans. Until recently, Senate Republicans had routinely approved Trump’s nominees for lifetime seats on district and appeals courts during his second term, confirming 57 so far and helping him cement a conservative imprint on the judiciary that will outlast his presidency. But as the White House and Senate Republican leaders press ahead with judicial nominees during the lame-duck session, a handful of Republicans have blocked or cast doubt on three nominees selected for their home states. Senators traditionally help choose judges for vacancies in their states. Trial court nominees are especially vulnerable because, under Senate custom, home-state senators can block them by withholding a “blue slip," a form indicating support to the Senate Judiciary Committee. While generally honoring that tradition, the White House has sometimes picked conservatives to fill judicial vacancies over the objections of Republican senators. "We put up a lot of really qualified candidates that we sent to the White House, and they basically ignored that and just put through their one," Senator Alan Armstrong, an Oklahoma Republican, said. Two outgoing Republican members on the Senate Judiciary Committee, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas, can deny such nominees the votes needed to advance. ’NOT THE WAY IT WORKS HERE’ The White House on Tuesday took the rare step of withdrawing US District Judge Lee Rudofsky’s nomination to the St. Louis-based 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals and replacing him with Arkansas Supreme Court Justice J. Cody Hiland after US Senators John Boozman and Tom Cotton of Arkansas opposed Rudofsky. Outgoing Republican Senators Armstrong and Cornyn have withheld public support for two nominees in their states, while Tillis has used his position on the committee to help block candidates opposed by his colleagues. Tillis, who has a fractured relationship with Trump, told reporters on Thursday that the White House has at times essentially told senators, "This is our guy, I hope you’ll get on board." "That’s not how it works here," he said. "They should expect they’re going to get this response." For the White House, the next few weeks reflect the last hurrah on a project that began during Trump’s first administration to shift the federal judiciary’s ideological balance to the right, an initiative whose effects will be felt for years after Trump leaves office. items.title: Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP control in states
items.excerpt: The midterm elections saw historic changes in state legislatures. Pennsylvania voters elected a Democratic majority in the state Senate for the first time since Jimmy Carter was president. Democrats in Texas will run the state House there for the first time in 24 years. The Georgia House will have a Democratic majority for the first time in more than 20 years. The results reversed a GOP dominance in legislatures that began in 2010 and had solidified since. Going into the midterms, Republicans controlled legislatures in 28 states and Democrats held 18. The remaining few were divided. Now, with some votes still being counted, it looks likely the Democrats will hold a 24-to-22 lead with others divided. So far, Democrats have picked up seats in nearly every state that held legislative elections, according to data compiled by NPR. Democrats gained significant ground in unexpected, reliably Republican states, like Texas, Utah and Florida. The shift could mean real change in people's lives as legislatures rewrite laws on taxes, reproductive rights, access to health care, school funding and other issues. Legislatures have also been important in promoting or blocking President Trump's agenda. ... Some of the biggest changes could come in states where Democrats now control both chambers of the legislature and the governor's office. They gained six new "trifectas." In Arizona, Democrats will have the majorities in the state House and Senate and hold the governor's office — a trifecta — for the first time since 1966. One possible policy change could be on school vouchers. Gov. Katie Hobbs has repeatedly tried to reform and limit the state's billion-dollar voucher program, which provides public money for private school tuition regardless of family income. But the Republican-run legislature had blocked her. Arizona Democrats have said they also hope to provide financial relief on rent, utilities and childcare. In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has promised to work with a newly Democratic legislature to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, strengthen abortion rights and increase affordable housing. Democrats also won trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and in Nevada, where they won the governor's office. They broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. Going into the midterms, Republicans had a few more trifectas than the Democrats. Now Democrats will likely have 22 and the Republicans 17, with 10 other states divided, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. (That doesn't include Nebraska, with a Republican governor and a unicameral legislature controlled by Republicans.) ### Democrats can break Republican momentum in some states In some states, including Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, Democrats have turned Republican-controlled legislatures into divided legislatures. Georgia Democrats won the House and came close in the Senate. On their agenda, they could try to win over a few GOP lawmakers and pass Medicaid expansion to provide health care to more low income residents. There could also be an effort by House Democrats to repeal that state's six-week abortion ban, but that could be a tough sell in the Senate. Democrats won control the North Carolina state House. As for the state Senate, a Republican is leading the race for one seat by just over a couple hundred votes and it is likely headed to a recount. It will determine if Republicans have a one-seat majority or if the chamber will be tied. If it is tied, the Democratic lieutenant governor would be the tie-breaker. North Carolina Democrats are expected to try and roll back some abortion restrictions. And Democratic Gov. Josh Stein has called on both parties to work on addressing affordability concerns once the legislature convenes. In several states, Democrats fell short of flipping some Republican-held chambers but won enough seats to end Republican supermajorities. The Multistate government relations firm says that happened in six states that had GOP, veto-proof supermajorities. That will matter most where there are Democratic governors, who now have leverage to veto GOP initiatives, like in North Carolina, Ohio and Kansas.

items.title: Ebenezer Box Office: Johnny Depp Movie Leads Over How to Rob a Bank
items.excerpt: Nov 15, 2026 8:20am PT # Box Office: Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to No. 1 With $19 Million, ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Stumbles With $5 Million Debut By Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter ... Johnny Depp returned to the top of box office charts as “ Ebenezer,” his new take on “A Christmas Carol,” collected a decent $19 million from 3,535 North American theaters in its opening weekend. Overseas, the PG-13 adaptation of the Charles Dickens classic has generated $23 million from 63 markets for a global start of $42 million. “Ebenezer” is notable as Depp’s first major movie role in eight years, since 2018’s “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald.” His career in Hollywood began to unravel in 2020 after allegations of domestic abuse leveled by his ex-wife Amber Heard (which he has denied) resulted in two high-profile defamation trials. Although his acting roles mostly dried up, a study conducted by the National Research Group in April 2026 indicated that Depp remained a popular figure across the globe. ... So how did that enthusiasm translate to “Ebenezer” in its first weekend of release? Analysts say tickets didn’t signal a resounding embrace amid Depp’s return to studio fare. However, the movie delivered a nice boost to theater owners ahead of Thanksgiving and looks to provide a sizable return on investment for Paramount. Given the uncertainty around Depp, the studio cautiously spent $38 million to produce the film. Depp was paid $5 million, a fraction of what he’s earned on prior studio movies, with the promise of bonuses tied to box office performance. ... Directed by West, known for the “X” horror trilogy, “Ebenezer” spins the oft-told tale of the cold-hearted businessman known as Scrooge as he’s visited by the ghosts of Christmas past, present and future. Though critics were harsh (it holds a 53% on Rotten Tomatoes), audiences awarded the movie a positive “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls. ... “How to Rob a Bank” didn’t make bank, stumbling at No. 7 with $5 million from 2,810 theaters in its debut. It also struggled internationally with $5.1 million from 73 territories, bringing its global total to a soft $10.3 million. The heist comedy, starring Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz and Pete Davidson, was produced for more than $40 million, and cinema operators keep about half of ticket sales. What’s troubling is neither critics nor audiences were receptive to the film, which landed a “B-” grade on CinemaScore and tepid 33% on Rotten Tomatoes. David Leitch directed the R-rated movie, which follows a crew of social media-savvy bank robbers who broadcast their daring heists, unaware their viral fame has caught the attention of the feds.

items.excerpt: - Nov 15, 2026 Updated 1 hr ago Phil Collins cries, Billy Idol shouts and rappers romp at Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony has been a lively celebration. Phil Collins gave a tearful acceptance speech, while Cynthia Erivo delivered an electrifying tribute. Oprah Winfrey inducted the late Luther Vandross, and Wu-Tang Clan brought a rowdy celebration to the stage. Queen Latifah, Oasis, MC Lyte, Sade, Joy Division/New Order, and Iron Maiden were also inducted. U2 surprised the audience by opening the night, and Run DMC and Aerosmith closed with a loud jam. Despite some absences, the event was vibrant and memorable, with performances and tributes that kept the crowd engaged. Glenn Close and Ridley Scott to get honorary Oscars at Governors Awards LOS ANGELES (AP) — Glenn Close will finally hold an Oscar and make an acceptance speech after eight nominations without a win. She will receive an honorary Academy Award for her five-decade career at the Governors Awards on Sunday night. Director Ridley Scott of films like “Alien” and “Gladiator” will also receive an honorary Oscar. He plans to accept via recorded video. Disney animator Floyd Norman and producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler will be honored too. Close shares the record with Peter O’Toole for the most nominations without a win. She has won other major awards throughout her long career, including Emmys, Golden Globes and Tonys. ... LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame has inducted its 2026 class of 18 musical legends at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. Phil Collins enters again for his solo career, inducted by Travis Barker. Wu-Tang Clan, inducted by Chris Rock, performed a medley of hits. ... Luther Vandross was honored by Oprah Winfrey, with Usher performing ... Rick Rubin, inducted by Neil Young, received the Musical Excellence Award. ... Richard Sterban, member of the celebrated country and gospel group The Oak Ridge Boys, dies at 83 Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist of the Grammy-award winning gospel quartet The Oak Ridge Boys and a country music hall of famer, has died. He was 83. His family and the band say he died Saturday in Hendersonville, Tennessee, due to complications from bronchitis and pneumonia after a long battle with cancer. Sterban was a native of New Jersey. He left his job as a backup singer for Elvis Presley to join the vocal group, best known perhaps for its rendition of “Elvira.” The band won five Grammy awards, and its members were inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015. In 2011 they gained membership in the Grand Ole Opry. Trailblazing film producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler make Governors Awards history Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, co-founders of Killer Films, are making history Sunday with their honorary Oscar at the Governors Awards. They are the first female producing team and independent producers to receive the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award. Known for bold, independent films like “Boys Don’t Cry” and “Safe,” they have produced over 100 films. Their work has been pivotal in New Queer Cinema and includes cult classics like “Hedwig and the Angry Inch.” Despite challenges, they remain optimistic and continue to create innovative films. They have a new project, “De Noche,” starring Pedro Pascal and Danny Ramirez. ... Bobby Pulido is a member-elect for the U.S. House of Representatives who has also recently won the Latin Grammy for best Tejano album. He accepted the award Thursday at a ceremony in Las Vegas that reflected a broader trend of political advocacy in music. Pulido recently won a competitive race to flip Texas’ 15th Congressional District. He announced his retirement from music onstage and other artists called for unity and representation. Daddy Yankee and Anitta highlighted issues in Puerto Rico and Brazil. Political references had long been dormant from the awards. ... Filipino singer Carmelle storms to victory in Eurovision Asia debut in Bangkok BANGKOK (AP) — Filipino singer Carmelle won the first Asian edition of the Eurovision Song Contest with a fiery performance of “Sobra-Sobra,” beating 10 other acts in the grand final in Bangkok. Votes from national juries and viewers worldwide determined the winner. Thai duo Mang x Daou placed second with “Aroma,” followed by Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên with “Em Tiên.” Contestants arrived on tuk-tuks, waving their national flags. Bulgarian singer Dara, winner of the 70th Eurovision Song Contest, performed as a special guest. The contest seeks to put music first, though it often faces political challenges.
